epoch: Ten months and eleven days after Collegium enrolment — evening
unit: Millions of constant-price Veyrasse lorrat-equivalents per local year

profiles.name: Veldrassen
profiles.specialties: Heavy engineering, railway equipment and general manufactures; coal and processed fuel exports
profiles.constraints: Provincial consent slows concentration; major arsenals and railway junctions remain irreplaceable targets.
profiles.older_arts: Court examination offices and provincial registries preserve records; access varies by patron.
profiles.description: The crown is a compact among old provinces: its armies and foundries are enormous, but provincial estates bargain over every exceptional levy. Rail contracts and coal exports hold the monarchy together more reliably than court ceremony.

food.name: Veldrassen
food.history: A composite crown includes humid lowlands, high terraces and temperate uplands; imperial-looking court service conceals many provincial kitchens.
food.everyday: Maize polenta with beans and mushroom gravy in the uplands; rice replaces maize in irrigated lowland districts.
food.hospitality: Braised beef with red wine and layered herb pasta; provincial delegates insist on different cheeses.
food.drink: Plateau beer, lowland cane drink and coffee at the court.
food.daily_life: Altitude matters as much as latitude. Mountain towns import much of their grain, while court menus display produce from every province as a claim to unity.

profiles.name: Ostrevain
profiles.specialties: Grain distribution, military stores and arsenal production
profiles.constraints: Mass manpower outstrips motor transport; imported precision machinery constrains arsenal expansion.
profiles.older_arts: Estate households preserve healing and harvest observances; arsenal physicians record unusual cases, usually through the patron who brings the subject to them.
profiles.description: Royal commissioners are consolidating an agricultural monarchy into an arsenal state. Landowners favour grain exports; army purchasers want controlled prices and labour for new factories. The resulting dispute reaches from village granaries to the court.

food.name: Ostrevain
food.history: Cereal estates, cattle districts and newly industrial towns trade large quantities of durable staples. Central purchasing has spread army dishes across provincial boundaries.
food.everyday: Pepper bean stew thickened with maize meal, with smoked beef on paydays.
food.hospitality: Stuffed roast fowl, squash dumplings and nut pastries.
food.drink: Brown beer and lightly fermented fruit drinks.
food.daily_life: Soldiers carry toasted grain and hard cheese; wealthy tables emphasise fresh meat and fruit that has not endured a convoy journey.

profiles.name: Rovessara
profiles.specialties: Precision instruments, electrical apparatus and overseas commerce
profiles.constraints: Trade interruption threatens fuel and food imports; its skilled workforce is difficult to replace.
profiles.older_arts: Institutes and hospitals collect documented cases; evidence is better organised than practitioner supply.
profiles.description: Merchant councils govern a commercial republic whose banks finance shipping and precision workshops. Foreign clients need its instruments and engines, but the republic depends on open sea lanes and negotiated access to raw materials.

food.name: Rovessara
food.history: Maritime commerce joins a mild western coast to upland cheese districts and distant spice markets. Restaurant fashion changes faster than village food.
food.everyday: Bean-and-greens soup with flatbread and olive oil; tiny fried fish at the quays.
food.hospitality: Rice cooked in seafood stock, fine stuffed pasta and chilled fruit creams in wealthy city cafés.
food.drink: Bitter coffee, aperitif wine and citrus cordial.
food.daily_life: Fresh oil, mountain butter and imported spice coexist rather than defining one uniform national cuisine. Ice houses and refrigerated warehouses support the richest urban tables.

profiles.name: Brannervaux
profiles.specialties: Water engineering, agricultural processing and industrial chemistry
profiles.constraints: Water allocation and estate vetoes complicate mobilisation; river freight is sensitive to damaged locks.
profiles.older_arts: Water boards retain old records of divination and flood omens beside their engineering archives. Practical credibility depends on repeated results, not an inherited title.
profiles.description: City charters, landed estates and river authorities divide power in a federation confined to its own basins. Locks, flood protection and water allocation bind members together while producing repeated disputes about who pays upstream and who benefits downstream.

food.name: Brannervaux
food.history: Unequal river cities share barges, mill customs and periodic floods. Grain, pulses and freshwater fish travel more readily than political loyalty.
food.everyday: Lentils with smoked carp and flat noodles; poorer bowls omit fish and add greens.
food.hospitality: River-fish dumplings in herb butter and plum-filled pastries.
food.drink: Pear cider, mild beer and roasted-barley drinks.
food.daily_life: Floodplain gardens supply onions and beans. Fish smoking and grain warehouses make the river ports vital even to communities beyond the floodplain.

profiles.name: Cervaud
profiles.specialties: Frontier logistics, armaments repair and estate agriculture
profiles.constraints: Arms and credit depend on competing patrons; prolonged mobilisation drains agricultural labour.
profiles.older_arts: Border houses keep private warding manuscripts and employ occasional itinerant readers. Rival patrons make access political and discourage sharing successful practice.
profiles.description: A hereditary border duchy buys security by bargaining with Veldrassen and Ostrevain. Its fortified frontier supports a substantial officer class; competing patrons and military purchasing make nominal independence expensive.

food.name: Cervaud
food.history: Border garrisons borrow cooking from both larger patrons, while local families argue over which dishes predate foreign influence.
food.everyday: Cabbage rolls stuffed with rice or barley and a little minced meat.
food.hospitality: Roast pork with sour cherries and crisp potato cakes.
food.drink: Dark beer, cherry spirit and heavily sweetened coffee for visitors.
food.daily_life: Ration bread and pickled vegetables dominate remote posts. Market-day sausages are a small luxury that survives frequent changes of uniform.

profiles.name: Veylac
profiles.specialties: Metallurgy, machine tools and factory production
profiles.constraints: Exposed frontier factories and food imports limit a long war despite excellent machine-tool output.
profiles.older_arts: Factory reading societies debate arcane reports alongside medicine and natural philosophy. Private experiments remain scattered, with no dependable industrial application.
profiles.description: An industrial republic governed through municipal and commercial representation, with a long argument over labour’s place in that settlement. Machine-tool exports pay for essential imports; disputed frontiers consume revenue that towns want spent on housing and power.

food.name: Veylac
food.history: Industrial towns link cooler uplands to river farms. Working households value meals that can be reheated when factory shifts end at different hours.
food.everyday: Baked beans beneath an onion-and-breadcrumb crust, with smoked sausage when affordable.
food.hospitality: Cheese-filled pasta browned in butter; orchard-fruit tart at civic dinners.
food.drink: Pale beer, plum cordial and café coffee.
food.daily_life: Cooperative dining rooms compete with private factory canteens. Imported coastal fish is popular but more expensive than the local root-and-grain staples.

profiles.name: Ossavren successor territories
profiles.specialties: Competing provincial administrations, workshops and military supply; divided coalfields and petroleum districts
profiles.constraints: Combined rival returns; no common treasury, staff or army. Rail gauges, tolls and civil fighting fragment capacity.
profiles.older_arts: The fallen crown’s collections are divided among rival courts and displaced teachers. Competing claims to authentic manuscripts matter more than any central school.
profiles.description: These are the successor territories of a broken crown, not a single nation. Rival palaces, provincial commands and autonomous ports divide its large coal and petroleum resources. Shared roads and kinship survive beneath customs barriers and foreign-backed claimants.

food.name: Ossavren successor territories
food.history: Former royal roads carried recipes across a realm now divided by customs barriers and rival armies. Shared dishes remain a language of kinship across hostile borders.
food.everyday: Red lentil pot with flatbread in warm valleys; barley-and-turnip broth in higher districts.
food.hospitality: Lamb with preserved lemon and almonds; former court households still serve rosewater rice pudding.
food.drink: Mint tea in warm valleys, mountain beer inland and sweet wine in surviving vineyard districts.
food.daily_life: Smuggling brings salt, oil and family recipes across front lines. An abundant banquet may conceal shortages in a neighbouring claimant’s territory.

profiles.name: Rovengard
profiles.specialties: Valley agriculture, timber and stronghold supply
profiles.constraints: Winter supply and dispersed valley garrisons consume most available transport.
profiles.older_arts: Valley households preserve protective rites and stories of gifted healers. Winter isolation keeps instruction local, and court inquiries rarely reach every settlement.
profiles.description: The southern valley monarchy holds the largest single government in Morholt. Its crown must secure food routes between farming basins and scattered fortresses; huge forest claims do not translate into a dense tax base or a freely deployable army.

food.name: Rovengard
food.history: Sheltered southern valleys support oats, rye, roots and dairy herds; forest preserves add berries and inspected game.
food.everyday: Rye-crust fish loaf with potato and onion, carried cold or warmed beside a stove.
food.hospitality: Venison with sour red berries and cream, followed by baked curd cheese.
food.drink: Small beer, berry cordial and hot herb infusions.
food.daily_life: A winter pantry matters more than a fashionable fresh ingredient. Household drying racks and communal bake days bind city relatives to valley farms.

profiles.name: Varnesk
profiles.specialties: Ore processing, specialist steels, bearings and durable machinery
profiles.constraints: Specialist foundries are strong; grain imports and seasonal routes make an extended blockade dangerous.
profiles.older_arts: Guarded workshops sometimes collaborate with rare practitioners; no standardised arcane production.
profiles.description: Mining councils and foundry proprietors govern a league rather than a royal province. Specialist steel and machinery create wealth, but imported food and negotiated convoy protection limit how far the league can act alone.

food.name: Varnesk
food.history: Mining leagues inherit northern preservation techniques but rely heavily on imported grain and valley dairy produce.
food.everyday: Potato-and-rye dumplings with smoked pork and fermented cabbage.
food.hospitality: Beef baked beneath a thick salt-and-rye crust, opened for foundry feasts.
food.drink: Dark rye beer; strong black tea bought through concession merchants.
food.daily_life: Canteens portion meat by shift entitlement. A late supply train can turn dumplings into thin flour soup without stopping the furnaces.

profiles.name: Galdresk
profiles.specialties: Field medicine, communications and scholarly traditions
profiles.constraints: Small arsenals and scattered teaching houses constrain scale; trained wardens excel locally rather than in mass campaigns.
profiles.older_arts: Small warden teaching houses preserve field traditions; skilled practitioners remain exceptionally rare.
profiles.description: A wardenship of chartered orders, estates and civilian towns. Houses of medicine and the older arts preserve useful learning without supplying a large magical army. Obligations of shelter and patrol compete with each district’s limited stores.

food.name: Galdresk
food.history: Order houses preserve remedies and practical cookery alongside the older arts. Most food is ordinary, nourishing and carefully stored.
food.everyday: Oat broth with roots, mushrooms and dried fish; kitchens adjust texture for the sick.
food.hospitality: Trout in cream with dill-like herbs, served with small sourdough loaves and berry compote.
food.drink: Unsweetened herbal tea and berry wine on feast days.
food.daily_life: Healing traditions do not make every herb magical. Supplies are dated and inspected; winter hospitality can impose a serious obligation on an isolated house.

profiles.name: Halskert
profiles.specialties: River freight, milling and agricultural exchange
profiles.constraints: Seasonal navigation and dependence on imported fuels limit sustained operations away from rivers.
profiles.older_arts: Pilots and mill communities preserve water omens and inherited household protections. Navigation still relies on soundings, charts and experienced crews.
profiles.description: River towns and mill proprietors govern a republic tied to seasonal navigation. Its food valleys are valuable to colder neighbours; spring flood control, pilotage and grain contracts dominate political bargaining.

food.name: Halskert
food.history: Seasonal river traffic sustains mills, fisheries and gardens in comparatively sheltered valleys. Boat families carry recipes between rival towns.
food.everyday: Barley baked with lake fish and onion in covered crocks.
food.hospitality: Butter-fried freshwater fish, green peas and a layered berry cake during the short summer.
food.drink: Oat beer and tart orchard cider where fruit grows.
food.daily_life: Smokehouses fill before freeze-up. Spring fish suppers mark reopened navigation and the arrival of news as much as the season’s catch.

profiles.name: Tervayne
profiles.specialties: Maritime freight, ship maintenance and naval supply
profiles.constraints: Sea lanes carry its power; inland movement is slow and there is no through railway to eastern Vesalius.
profiles.older_arts: Port archives collect travellers’ accounts and sea traditions; private patrons sponsor a few readers, whose conflicting methods do not form a naval service.
profiles.description: A western Vesalian maritime power whose interests face the western ocean. Roughly two thousand kilometres of uplands and intervening governments separate its principal sphere from Veyrasse; it competes with eastern merchants overseas without sharing their local frontier.

food.name: Tervayne
food.history: Western ports face a different trading sea from Veyrasse and share more food traffic with southern islands and Otrantian merchants.
food.everyday: Fish-and-potato bake beneath an oat crust, with pickled onions.
food.hospitality: Mussels in cream and white wine, followed by baked custard scented with imported spice.
food.drink: Coastal cider, amber beer and port-house coffee.
food.daily_life: Sailors’ inexpensive meals favour salted fish; fresh shellfish signals a short journey from water to table. Inland villages are less maritime than the national reputation suggests.

profiles.name: Vardol
profiles.specialties: Northern arsenals, estate production and military provisioning; coalfields and fuel refining
profiles.constraints: The Averholt frontier and northern garrisons tie down formations; large armies cannot simply redeploy to the Marches.
profiles.older_arts: Military physicians record unusual perception when it comes to their attention. Household and estate traditions survive outside those files, often deliberately.
profiles.description: A northern realm of arsenals, fuel processing and grain districts. Rivalry with Averholt and the bargaining power of military suppliers occupy its government. Road access to Caldrienne exists, but does not turn the eastern Marches into a Vardolian province.

food.name: Vardol
food.history: Refinery and arsenal towns share a strong canteen tradition with their farming hinterland. Winter provisions matter more inland than at the ports.
food.everyday: Rye parcels filled with potato, onion and smoked sausage, baked in communal ovens.
food.hospitality: Beef in dark beer with prune gravy and steamed bread; elaborate layered honey cake.
food.drink: Rye beer and sour cherry cordial.
food.daily_life: Shift whistles govern supper in the industrial wards. Kitchen gardens and pickled cabbage cushion disruptions to the grain trains.

profiles.name: Averholt
profiles.specialties: Basin agriculture, internal trade and provincial engineering
profiles.constraints: Provincial bargains and the Vardol frontier absorb resources; interior transport has limited spare capacity.
profiles.older_arts: Provincial collections preserve distinct healing and warding customs. Teachers exchange access through local patrons rather than a realm-wide curriculum.
profiles.description: An inland realm held together by provincial arrangements and productive basins. It contests influence with Vardol and trades through defended passes toward Karsenne. Provincial councils resist campaigns that would strip local defences to fund distant annexations.

food.name: Averholt
food.history: Provincial land bargains preserve different kitchens inside the same realm; grain taxes and shared fairs link the basins.
food.everyday: Barley risotto with mushrooms and hard cheese; peasant versions use dripping instead of butter.
food.hospitality: Stuffed river pike and pastry filled with poppy seed, served when a provincial house receives important guests.
food.drink: Apple wine in orchard districts; malt beer in the colder basins.
food.daily_life: Public ovens are meeting places as well as fuel economies. A dispute over milling rights can be discussed for an entire supper without anyone naming its political purpose.

profiles.name: Serevask Republic
profiles.specialties: Civil administration, filtration and chemical workshops, repair shops and commercial services
profiles.constraints: The republic controls only its own districts. Varnelle, Kelbrun and Gavrel have separate forces and revenues; old charter claims confer no authority over them.
profiles.older_arts: Republican archives retain fragments of the former basin federation’s case records. Its clerks cannot compel the successor authorities to supply missing material.
profiles.description: The Serevask Republic administers thirteen million people around its surviving civic and industrial districts. It is the remnant of a southern customs federation, never a continental government. Varnelle, Kelbrun and Gavrel administer their own territory, taxation and armed forces. The old federal charter remains an argument over debt and water, not effective authority over them.

food.name: Serevask Republic
food.history: The old Serevask customs federation joined four southern basins, never Vesalius as a whole. Its divided successors still recognise one another’s dishes.
food.everyday: Serevask sour rice: rice and lentils finished with soured milk, toasted seed and browned onion.
food.hospitality: Duck with bitter orange, accompanied by layered rice scented with preserved peel.
food.drink: Strong black tea; fermented rice drink at harvest gatherings.
food.daily_life: The remnant government maintains public grain kitchens near its ministries. Former federal recipes outlast the tax union, while each successor claims its own version is the original.

profiles.name: Varnelle
profiles.specialties: Delta freight, customs, filtration and processing trades
profiles.constraints: Delta channels, customs dependence and disputed upstream water access constrain resilience.
profiles.older_arts: River pilots and household healers trade practical lore around the delta. Port boards occasionally investigate a useful claim without endorsing an entire tradition.
profiles.description: The delta authorities gained effective independence from Serevask as rebuilding debts and customs disputes broke the old basin federation. Port and water boards bargain with merchants and troops; river access makes their policies consequential far upstream.

food.name: Varnelle
food.history: Delta rice, fisheries and freight markets furnished the former federation’s export table; incoming crews introduced sour, hot and sweet condiments.
food.everyday: Varnelle red rice with river fish, pepper and beans, cooked in one broad pan.
food.hospitality: Crab broth with fine rice noodles and citrus leaf; confectioners sell sesame brittle.
food.drink: Iced citrus water where ice can be bought; tea and light cane spirit.
food.daily_life: Fish sauce is an everyday seasoning rather than a luxury. Flood years alter rice prices across all four successor states.

profiles.name: Kelbrun
profiles.specialties: Upriver freight, plantation produce and agricultural machinery
profiles.constraints: Plantation levies are numerous but unevenly equipped; imported engines and fuel remain essential.
profiles.older_arts: Estate remedies coexist with workers’ inherited protective practices. Private collections are accessible through personal trust, while plantation authorities are wary of independent followings.
profiles.description: Upriver councils and plantation interests govern separately from Serevask. Rubber chemistry, filtration and agricultural exports bring revenue, while estate labour obligations and downstream water demands provoke persistent disputes.

food.name: Kelbrun
food.history: Upriver gardens and plantation labour communities mix basin rice dishes with tubers, legumes and orchard fruit.
food.everyday: Steamed tuber cakes with black beans and a sharp herb relish.
food.hospitality: Pork braised in cane syrup and sour fruit; rice cakes filled with ground nuts for festivals.
food.drink: Roasted-grain coffee substitutes and cane spirit; estate houses serve imported coffee.
food.daily_life: Labourers eat at field shelters from wrapped parcels. Plantation owners’ lavish fruit tables conceal the uneven access to meat and purchased grain.

profiles.name: Gavrel
profiles.specialties: March provisioning, rural estates and frontier workshops
profiles.constraints: Household loyalties divide command; repair workshops cannot replace large losses of imported equipment.
profiles.older_arts: March houses preserve family books of omens and protections. Their secrecy divides instruction as effectively as the frontier divides military command.
profiles.description: Chartered march houses retain their own levies and recognise only limited common obligations. Their earlier partnership in the southern federation left shared debts and roads, not obedience to Serevask. Small industrial centres depend on negotiated access through their neighbours.

food.name: Gavrel
food.history: March-house kitchens descend from basin customs but favour portable grain and smoked provisions for retainers travelling between estates.
food.everyday: Millet cakes with goat stew and sour plum relish.
food.hospitality: Spit-roasted kid with nut paste, followed by dense dried-fruit bread.
food.drink: Sour milk, herbal tea and plum wine.
food.daily_life: Hospitality includes bread broken by the host, but its quality distinguishes an honoured guest from a hired messenger. Poor tenants substitute lentils for goat.

profiles.name: Bellacosta Cantons
profiles.specialties: Tropical produce, timber concessions, harbour handling and coastal escorts
profiles.constraints: Canton tolls and planter credit divide the export trade. Escort flotillas answer to their sponsors; the combined manpower is not one army.
profiles.older_arts: Canton healers inherit plant lore and protective observances. Port subscribers occasionally pay to compare case records, but inland custodians resist giving away family knowledge.
profiles.description: The cantons grew out of harbour and plantation charters left without a royal guarantor after the Long Culling. Jougrenne convenes the coastal toll assembly; Nantac administers a separate inland land court. Neither can tax the other’s households. Harbour dues fund escorts while plantation owners pay for roads and demand control of the checkpoints. Veldrassen buys tropical produce and timber here, but its purchasing agents face competing canton tariffs rather than a single ministry. Tenant disputes centre on debt and access to cleared farmland; the assembly meets over commercial quarrels, not to command a national army.

food.name: Bellacosta Cantons
food.everyday: Rice cooked in coconut milk accompanies peppered fish near the coast; inland labourers eat cassava cakes and bean relish. At Jougrenne, prosperous hosts serve fish wrapped in aromatic leaves, followed by cane syrup fritters. Sour fruit drinks and weak cane beer are ordinary; imported wine belongs to charter banquets.

profiles.government: Coastal canton assemblies and inland land courts; shared toll negotiations, separate treasuries and troops.

profiles.name: Cavressa Principalities
profiles.specialties: Wool, preserved provisions, upland cartage and small estate workshops
profiles.constraints: Rights of passage change between courts. Winter fodder and incompatible toll privileges limit concentration more than nominal levy strength.
profiles.older_arts: Court chapbooks mix household wards with dynastic histories. Independent practitioners move between patrons and market fairs, carrying techniques that rival courts claim as their own.
profiles.description: A chain of small courts and charter towns occupies the southwestern approaches. Collengo’s market charter protects merchants from estate levies, while the lords around Peregia claim payment for escorting their wagons. Winter fodder and access through the uplands matter more than distant dynastic titles. Albaret brokers wool and preserved food between the courts. Marriage contracts frequently change toll rights without moving a border; merchants employ local advocates to interpret them. Southern sea trade offers an alternative to the roads, but only to houses able to finance a shipment.

food.name: Cavressa Principalities
food.everyday: Barley noodles with browned cabbage are everyday food in the cooler districts. Shepherds carry hard cheese and sour rye loaves; court cooks serve mutton with dried plums and a crust of toasted grain. Albaret inns are known for pear pastries. Dark beer and plum spirit travel better than fresh milk.

profiles.government: Independent principalities, free market charters and estate courts; no common sovereign.

profiles.name: Vaulcerre Basin Leagues
profiles.specialties: Irrigated grain, mill machinery, fertiliser works and inland water freight
profiles.constraints: Water commands hold separate troops. A damaged gate or withheld release can disable production without an invading army taking the towns.
profiles.older_arts: Reservoir communities preserve water-divining traditions. Boards test useful claims against measured flows; most inherited observances remain unverified.
profiles.description: Anselleuil’s reservoir command, Jarnan’s commercial council and the estate assemblies around Votane share a drainage basin but not a government. Their water compact survived the destruction of the authority that first imposed it. Gates must open in an agreed order; delaying an upstream release can destroy a downstream planting season. Brannervaux engineers are employed as arbitrators and suspected of favouring their own merchants. Grain barges, mill repair and fertiliser works sustain the towns. Disputes usually begin as inspections, impoundments and unpaid maintenance bills before soldiers become involved.

food.name: Vaulcerre Basin Leagues
food.everyday: Millet porridge with greens and groundnut sauce feeds field crews; fish dried beside the canals enriches stews. Jarnan serves spiced rice with river fish on market days. Fermented grain drink is inexpensive, while sweet tea signals a household with access to imported leaves. Drought changes recipes before it changes official water allocations.

profiles.government: Three principal water authorities with smaller charter towns; a binding water compact but no unified army.

profiles.name: Seravelle Littoral
profiles.specialties: Export warehousing, coastal shipping, food processing and commercial credit
profiles.constraints: Port conventions facilitate cargo, not military command. Inland debt disputes and foreign shipping insurance expose the region to commercial pressure.
profiles.older_arts: Harbour families collect foreign protective charms and accounts of unusual perception. Commercial correspondence circulates stories faster than competent teachers.
profiles.description: Astrellac’s harbour republic and the inland estate courts share the eastern littoral with smaller free ports. Their commercial convention standardises bills of lading but leaves taxes and criminal law local. Shipping families advance money against harvests; rural houses resent foreclosures by creditors who never leave the coast. Rovessaran insurers and instrument makers are influential customers. Port patrols cooperate against raiders, yet seize one another’s cargo when a debt dispute turns political. Hinterland towns depend on export warehouses for salt, tools and credit, which gives the harbours power beyond their formal borders.

food.name: Seravelle Littoral
food.everyday: Astrellac cooks fish in tomato and fennel broth and lays yesterday’s bread beneath it. Bean-filled pastries and olives travel inland with merchants. Wealthy harbour tables add citrus-roasted poultry and almond cakes; dockworkers buy chickpea fritters. Coastal wine is plentiful locally, while coffee is sold in small, strong cups.

profiles.government: Harbour republics and estate courts linked by a maritime commercial convention.

profiles.name: Haldrevik Concessions
profiles.specialties: Coal export concessions, timber, extraction machinery and contract transport
profiles.constraints: Company forces protect particular assets. Charter disputes, imported food and dependence on Varnesk equipment undermine any combined mobilisation.
profiles.older_arts: Mining crews preserve warning rites and private accounts of uncanny perception. Concession managers value a useful warning but rarely fund research that might interrupt extraction.
profiles.description: Concession houses hold time-limited rights to timber, minerals and fuel rather than sovereignty over every inhabitant. Asanetz keeps the surviving charter archive; Alauvenne houses one of the armed inspection posts. A house can own a railway and still owe rent to the community beneath it. Varnesk firms provide machinery and credit, exchanging technical dependence for preferred ore contracts. Charter renewals provoke strikes, armed intimidation and lawsuits over restoration bonds. Settlements outside a concession bargain for patrols in return for provisions; a company’s withdrawal can be more frightening than its arrival.

food.name: Haldrevik Concessions
food.everyday: Workers eat oat flatbread, pea soup and smoked fish at company canteens. Mushroom pies and berry preserves mark a well-stocked household. Managers import white flour and wine for renewal dinners; crews drink malt beer or roasted-grain coffee. An interrupted supply convoy can make the company shop the only source of food and deepen wage debt.

profiles.government: Rival concession houses under separate charters; settlement councils retain residence and market law.

profiles.name: Dreissen Wardholds
profiles.specialties: Convoy staging, cold-weather stores, fortress repair and imported-grain distribution
profiles.constraints: Most personnel guard their own supply districts. Winter fuel and food reserves impose strict limits on campaigning beyond the wardholds.
profiles.older_arts: Hospices hold copied warding and healing texts obtained from Galdresk visitors. The copies outnumber people able to demonstrate any effect.
profiles.description: Dananske, Dreinvar and Ferorvik anchor separate wardholds along the northern approaches. Each warden owes shelter to the villages that provision a fortress, but the obligation is disputed when stores run short. Their annual muster negotiates convoy schedules and exchanges hostages against broken promises; it does not elect a king. Galdresk medical houses maintain small hospices by invitation. Imported grain is strategically more important than ceremonial claims to the iceward interior. Officers measure influence in serviceable engines and winter stores, while civilian assemblies try to keep temporary requisitions from becoming permanent rent.

food.name: Dreissen Wardholds
food.everyday: Rye-and-oat bread, dried fish and sour cabbage dominate fortress kitchens. Venison is a costly addition to barley stew, not an everyday entitlement. Festival tables offer potato dumplings with browned butter and tart berry sauce. Hot malt drinks and strong grain spirit accompany winter hospitality; fuel scarcity limits baking as much as flour scarcity does.

profiles.government: Independent fortress wardens bound to civilian provisioning charters and a seasonal convoy muster.

profiles.name: Varneselle Estates
profiles.specialties: Fishing, timber, estate workshops and seasonal coastal freight
profiles.constraints: Port and estate forces obey different officers. Agricultural limits and dependence on Halskert grain make freight disruption especially costly.
profiles.older_arts: Fishing households and estate infirmaries preserve separate traditions. Port scribes collect storm accounts; families conceal gifts they fear a landlord might appropriate.
profiles.description: The eastern estates descend from competing settlement grants, with Varkessant’s port charter carved out of the landed claims. Estate bailiffs administer courts and patrol obligations; the port elects its own commercial officers. Fishing communities resist attempts to classify their customary shore access as a landlord’s concession. Halskert buys fish and timber and sells grain, giving its merchants leverage in disputes over freight. Family alliances cross estate borders, but succession cases repeatedly fragment holdings. Seasonal workers move between shore crews and inland workshops, carrying news faster than the formal post.

food.name: Varneselle Estates
food.everyday: Fish baked under a rye crust is shared along the shore; inland tables favour potato cakes with cultured cream and mushrooms. A formal estate meal adds roast poultry and sour-berry pudding. Small beer accompanies workday suppers, while herb spirits are offered to guests. The port’s fresh bread distinguishes it from outlying households that bake only when fuel permits.

profiles.government: Hereditary estate courts, independent fishing charters and Varkessant’s municipal port government.

profiles.name: Bressavelle Marches
profiles.specialties: Textile finishing, estate produce, bonded warehousing and wagon repair
profiles.constraints: Foreign clients subsidise rival toll houses. Local garrisons cannot be added together as an expeditionary force without renegotiating their obligations.
profiles.older_arts: Travelling readers find patrons among rival march houses. Books cross borders as gifts or contraband, leaving local collections partial and politically guarded.
profiles.description: The western marches form a belt of fortified lordships, town liberties and cultivated valleys between larger powers. Temevaux’s command guards a road junction; Malinne’s council controls a different customs district. Neither speaks for the entire belt. Tervayne merchants finance road repairs in exchange for bonded warehouses, while inland patrons subsidise rival toll houses. Small rulers survive by alternating clients and keeping neighbouring courts divided. Textile finishing, estate agriculture and wagon repair support a population far larger than its thinly charted principal towns suggest. A traveller’s permit may be valid for one bridge and useless at the next.

food.name: Bressavelle Marches
food.everyday: Households bake bean-and-onion pies and stretch broth with torn bread. Market inns serve pork with apples and coarse mustard; better tables add freshwater fish in butter and herb sauce. Cider is common in orchard districts, ale elsewhere. Customs officers are notorious for accepting imported coffee as hospitality while charging duty on the next sack.

profiles.government: Fortified lordships and town liberties; overlapping foreign patronage, no regional crown.

profiles.name: Vallessia Cantons
profiles.specialties: Grain storage, warm-climate produce, food processing and inter-canton brokerage
profiles.constraints: Military governors and elected market boards compete for transport and stores. Requisition disputes can immobilise a nominally available reserve.
profiles.older_arts: Granary towns maintain household protection rites alongside practical medicine. Market festivals bring teachers together briefly, without creating a permanent regional academy.
profiles.description: Southern market cantons rebuilt around local granaries after the Long Culling. Margeuil’s elected grain board, Darnenne’s military governor and the landed councils around Galigny compete over transport dues. Common measures for grain survived; a common treasury did not. Merchants connect warm lowland crops with cooler interior districts, using brokers who can guarantee passage through several authorities. Kelbrun buyers seek plantation produce and seasonal labour. Municipal councils resist the governors’ claim that every warehouse is a military asset, particularly after poor harvests make requisitions politically dangerous.

food.name: Vallessia Cantons
food.everyday: Rice-and-bean dishes with sharp green relish are common in the warmer cantons; upland tables add maize bread and soft cheese. Galigny market stalls sell stuffed peppers when in season. Feast days bring roast poultry with sour fruit, and sweet fritters. Light beer and fruit cordials are ordinary; imported coffee is concentrated in commercial houses.

profiles.government: Market cantons, landed councils and surviving military governorships; a common weights agreement only.

profiles.name: Rivessac Coast
profiles.specialties: Pilotage, coastal provisions, fishing and inland agricultural markets
profiles.constraints: Small communes lack a shared naval command. Poorly charted harbours, seasonal labour and interrupted inland roads limit the usable export surplus.
profiles.older_arts: Pilot families pass down sea omens and protective marks. Inland healers keep different records, and neither tradition offers a reliable substitute for ordinary seamanship or medicine.
profiles.description: Saultac is the best-charted inland market in a southeastern coastal region of small port communes and hereditary agricultural districts. The survey’s single principal marker is not its only inhabited place. Pilots’ guilds set practical terms for coastal travel; inland houses control cultivated land and the roads supplying the harbours. Ceralte brokers buy provisions here without governing the coast. Rival communes share storm warnings but guard their harbour soundings. The region’s political disputes concern port fees, seasonal labour and who funds guarded access to inland markets, rather than a single national succession.

food.name: Rivessac Coast
food.everyday: Coastal kitchens combine fish, white beans, garlic and local greens; inland families make herb dumplings and barley bread. Saultac’s market speciality is poultry braised with olives and sour citrus. Hosts offer almond biscuits with coffee when they can afford it; diluted wine or herbal infusions are more usual. Fresh fish becomes a luxury only a short disrupted journey inland.

profiles.government: Port communes and agricultural districts linked by pilotage agreements; separate administrations.

profiles.name: Karsenne Compact
profiles.specialties: Mining, military engineering and defended-pass supply
profiles.constraints: Strong pass defence and mining; food and coastal export access depend on neighbours. Councils control separate contingents.
profiles.older_arts: Mining communities preserve protective marks, warning dreams and accounts of unusual perception underground. Council archives collect accidents; practical instruction remains within small trusted circles.
profiles.description: Drossane hosts common business for autonomous mining councils and fortress districts. The Compact is a federation rather than a unified hereditary realm. Ores, engineering skills and defended approaches sustain its bargaining power, but coastal freight charges consume export income. Valley workshops and cultivated pockets support the upland economy. Veyrasse remains an uneasy defensive partner and vital outlet. A direct railway toward Calvernis is sought, not operating; existing roads do not provide an equivalent bulk-freight service.

food.name: Karsenne Compact
food.history: Pass commerce carried dairy and grain dishes between otherwise stubbornly independent mining councils. Food is compact enough for a shift or a winter ascent.
food.everyday: Drossane cheese dumplings: stale bread, sharp mountain cheese and onion, browned and served in broth.
food.hospitality: Covered rye pie of smoked goat and mushrooms; the richest versions have a deep butter crust.
food.drink: Whey drinks and small beer during work; juniper spirit after the shift.
food.daily_life: Lower valleys supply potatoes and cabbage, upland pastures cheese. Bought flour and coastal salt become costly when freight negotiations fail.

profiles.name: Duchy of Caldrienne
profiles.specialties: Agriculture, artillery production and armoured-vehicle workshops
profiles.constraints: Largest eastern tank arm, but fuel imports and the armed truce impose costs; offensive forces cannot strip all garrisons.
profiles.older_arts: Estate collections and military medical records preserve different accounts of unusual gifts. Ducal patronage can secure access, but also encourages custodians to conceal what they hold.
profiles.description: Valdrec houses the ducal administration and principal army depots. Productive valleys support estate agriculture and armament towns; the state fields strong infantry, artillery and a comparatively large armoured force. Ducal supervision is more centralised than in Veyrasse, though estate and arsenal interests still compete for resources. The unresolved Cressault claim strains an armed truce. Northern obligations and imports of Karsenne ore prevent its government from directing every resource against the March.

food.name: Duchy of Caldrienne
food.history: Agricultural estates feed the northern arsenals; ducal kitchens and barracks draw on the same cattle and grain districts at very different prices.
food.everyday: Valdrec sour-pot: cabbage, potato and beef simmered with caraway; soldiers receive more cabbage and less beef.
food.hospitality: Roast goose with apple stuffing and buckwheat cakes, served at estate weddings and officers’ banquets.
food.drink: Dark malt beer; plum spirit poured in small glasses.
food.daily_life: Army purchasing can empty market stalls before a mobilisation. Housewives argue over whether a proper sour-pot should contain tomato, an imported coastal habit.

profiles.name: March of Veyrasse
profiles.specialties: Railway engineering, port trade and municipal industry
profiles.constraints: Chartered houses, municipal funding and freight bottlenecks constrain command; machinery and fuel imports matter.
profiles.older_arts: Private circles and inherited manuscripts sustain the older arts outside the Collegium’s main priorities. Proven gifts are rare; most scholars judge claims cautiously rather than treating every charm as effective.
profiles.description: The charter balances the Margrave, landed houses, municipal councils and industrial proprietors. Auvrienne holds the court and government; Serravonne is a secondary port and rail junction. Coastal agriculture and workshops depend on inland ores and imported machinery. Railway unions can disrupt mobilisation, and poorer households bear disproportionate service obligations. Caldrienne remains the principal territorial rival; Karsenne is an essential supplier, while Calvernis and Ceralte provide competing maritime connections. The Margrave commands the standing army and foreign relations, while chartered institutions provide much of the money, manpower and transport. Education and engineering offer advancement through patronage. Railway superintendent Leont Vardesca governs railway affairs and dependants, not Serravonne’s government or army.

food.name: March of Veyrasse
food.history: Old coastal markets and the railway labour settlements exchange recipes with Caldrienne and Calvernis despite customs quarrels.
food.everyday: Ressant pot: white beans, leeks and barley, enriched with smoked pork when wages permit. Railway kitchens keep it warm for staggered shifts.
food.hospitality: Auvrienne veal in mustard cream, with buttered noodles; pear pastries follow at prosperous tables.
food.drink: Chicory coffee in workshops; real coffee, apple cider and dry valley wine in better-supplied houses.
food.daily_life: Fresh fish is ordinary near Serravonne, expensive uphill after a disrupted train. Station households stretch yesterday’s bread into broth dumplings.

profiles.name: Calvernis Republic
profiles.specialties: Shipping, banking, shipyards and maritime manufactures
profiles.constraints: Strong finance and convoy support; imported food and fuel expose it to interdiction and merchant-family disputes.
profiles.older_arts: Merchant households collect texts through maritime contacts. Private teaching and discreet patronage flourish more readily than a publicly accountable academy.
profiles.description: Miravelle is the seat of a republic whose restricted franchise favours shipping, banking and industrial families. Harbour revenues, ship maintenance and manufacturing support convoy escorts, coastal guns, marines and maritime aircraft. Smaller towns supply its commercial ports without erasing rival patronage networks. Veyrasse is a customer and competitor; an alternative outlet for Karsenne could redirect freight and toll income. No agreement has completed that proposed railway.

food.name: Calvernis Republic
food.history: The banking ports absorbed recipes from their merchant crews, while inland households retained grain-and-bean cooking.
food.everyday: Miravelle fish pot: firm coastal fish, onions, white beans and wine broth, ladled over yesterday’s bread.
food.hospitality: Saffron rice with shellfish and a separately served herb oil; expensive spice marks a host’s means.
food.drink: Dry white wine, anise cordial and strong coffee.
food.daily_life: Dockside stalls sell fried small fish in paper. A merchant’s citrus preserves may have travelled farther than the guests eating them.

profiles.name: Ceralte Admiralty
profiles.specialties: Coastal trade, fishing, naval maintenance and convoy services
profiles.constraints: Experienced coastal crews and minelayers; small population, grain imports and fuel dependence rule out a large land war.
profiles.older_arts: Maritime traditions and itinerant teachers preserve fragmentary practice; crews cannot rely on a gifted escort.
profiles.description: Dalmor is the fortified harbour and seat of a hereditary protector, senior naval council and island governors. Fishing, pilotage, convoy services and repair yards sustain the chain, while imported grain remains essential. Torpedo craft, mine warfare and knowledge of difficult waters offset limited land resources. Island communities depend on shipping rather than a mainland-style road network. Treaty cooperation coexists with accusations of privateering; no allegation proves official sponsorship.

food.name: Ceralte Admiralty
food.history: Limited grain land and long sea passages made imported flour, preserved fish and safe drinking water matters of government.
food.everyday: Dalmor soaked biscuit: ship’s bread softened with fish broth, oil and onions; ashore it gains tomatoes and herbs.
food.hospitality: Whole baked rockfish under a salt crust, opened at the table; almond-and-citrus cakes for shore leave and family feasts.
food.drink: Weak beer, diluted island wine and lemon syrup when supplies allow.
food.daily_life: Islanders know several preparations of the same catch. Grain shortages change the size of a loaf before they change a naval ration.

qualifications.valuation: Output is annual domestic value added, expressed at a common local purchasing-power valuation. It is neither treasury cash nor foreign currency exchange. Local currencies remain distinct.
qualifications.uncertainty: Rounded staff estimates: national output and personnel commonly vary by about 15 percent; equipment and fragmented jurisdictions by 25 percent or more. No estimate guarantees an outcome.
qualifications.forces: Standing personnel include active services, permanent garrisons, cadres and obligated household troops once. Additional trained reserves exclude serving personnel and untrained population. Sustainable field strength is the standing-force portion supportable away from fixed defences over roughly ninety days on established supply routes; it includes support staff and is not all riflemen.
qualifications.equipment: Armour means serviceable tanks and armoured cars, not all military vehicles. Aircraft are combat, reconnaissance and maritime types, excluding trainers. Artillery excludes infantry mortars. Fleet displacement totals commissioned combat vessels including coastal and river craft, excluding merchant ships; tonnage alone does not establish fighting quality.
qualifications.technology: 1: basic local repair; 2: established older production; 3: mature current manufacture; 4: advanced specialist production; 5: leading reproducible practice. Ratings measure industrial depth, not access to every invention. Readiness, logistics and cohesion use 1 (weak) to 5 (exceptional).
qualifications.coverage: Food and fuel coverage compare normal domestic annual supply to normal domestic consumption; above 100 percent permits exports. These are not stored months of supply, and import partners or transport may fail. National food and fuel returns reconcile against planetary production. Fuel is coal-equivalent energy and food is grain-equivalent nourishment; these aggregates do not make fuel grades or foods interchangeable. Distribution losses and reserve replenishment absorb the modest global surplus.
qualifications.scope: Ossavren and smaller-jurisdiction entries are geographic sums across separate authorities, not united states. Cressault is already within Veyrasse population and resources; the disputed corridor has no additional national army or treasury. Serevask counts loyal districts only.
qualifications.updates: Return epoch matches the current census. Annual output trend describes ordinary net capacity change, not guaranteed growth. War, closures, purges, investment, losses and political changes require revised returns.
